summary: A 1974 report on experiments with host output buffers on the Multics system to improve file transfer speed over the ARPANET. It is a practical note about tuning, not a protocol specification.

eli5.summary: A computer sending files was slow because of how it packed data to send. This note tried different ways to pack it and see if the transfers sped up.

subtitle: Faster file transfer for Multics over the ARPANET by increasing buffer size

tldr.problem: Multics could only send small 1012-bit messages on the ARPANET because its output buffers were too small, limiting file transfer speed to about 6,800 bits per second.
tldr.mechanism: The Multics team increased the IMP DIM output buffers from 940 bits to 8096 bits (the maximum the network allowed), letting it send larger messages in one go and reducing protocol overhead.
tldr.outcome: File transfer speed improved to about 27,600 bits per second, a four-fold gain. This showed that better buffer management could significantly improve network performance.

today: RFC 662 is Unknown status, not a protocol specification but a technical report on a successful tuning experiment from 1974. The approach of adaptive buffer sizing based on usage patterns influenced later protocol implementations.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: RFC 662 reports on an experiment with the Multics system at Project MAC, which was connected to the ARPANET to share system tapes with another Multics system. File transfer was painfully slow, taking about half an hour to move a typical system tape (roughly 12 million bits). The team suspected the problem lay in how Multics buffered data for network transmission.
sections.eli5: A computer called Multics needed to send big files across the network, but it was very slow. The people running it tried to find out why.

sections.title: The Buffer Problem
sections.content:
Multics used very small output buffers in its IMP Device Interface Manager. Each buffer could hold only 940 bits of data. When combined with a 72-bit header added by the network, this meant Multics sent messages of 1012 bits—a single network packet. The ARPANET could accept messages up to 8096 bits, so Multics was using only about one-eighth of the available space per message. This created excessive overhead: many tiny messages instead of a few larger ones.

Additionally, Multics strictly followed an older version of the IMP-to-Host protocol that required waiting for a Request-for-Next-Message (RFNM) response before sending the next message. Even though the protocol had been relaxed, the conservative approach meant delays between successive messages.
sections.eli5: Multics packed data into tiny boxes to send, even though the network could take much bigger boxes. This meant more boxes had to go back and forth, creating delays.

sections.title: The Solution and Results
sections.content:
The solution was straightforward: increase the output buffer size. Multics was modified to use two kinds of buffers. Small buffers (for interactive users sending small amounts of data) and large buffers (capable of holding the full 8096-bit message size for bulk file transfers). When a file transfer was detected, a large buffer was chosen automatically.

An experiment was conducted between MIT's Multics service machine and CISL's development machine. Files of about 2.5 million bits were transferred. The results were dramatic: the old system achieved 6,837 bits per second, while the new system achieved 27,578 bits per second—a four-fold improvement. With this improvement rate, a typical system tape of 12.5 million bits could be transmitted in about 7 minutes and 30 seconds instead of half an hour. Simultaneous transfers showed bandwidth sharing, with two concurrent transfers each reaching about 20,000 bits per second.
sections.eli5: When they made the boxes bigger, files moved four times faster. A file that took half an hour now took just seven and a half minutes.
